passage:
I'm Trisha, and my brother Francis is five. Today at Grandma's he looked at the sweet jar, then at the kitchen door where Mum was on the phone, then back at Grandma. "Mum said I can have two," he told her, very seriously.
Mum hadn't said anything. I was right there. But the funny thing was his face: he was watching Grandma really carefully, like checking whether she could tell.
Grandma smiled. "Let's ask Mum together." Francis's ears went pink. "Maybe she said one," he mumbled.

qa.q: What did Francis tell Grandma?
qa.a: Francis told her, "Mum said I can have two."

qa.q: How was Francis feeling as he watched Grandma so carefully?
qa.a: Francis was nervous about being caught, watching Grandma closely to check whether she could tell that Mum hadn't said anything.

qa.q: What did Grandma do that worked well?
qa.a: She calmly suggested asking Mum together, which checked the claim without scolding him.

qa.q: How does Trisha see her brother's fib?
qa.a: Trisha finds it funny and notices him testing Grandma, seeing it as something he is figuring out rather than being bad.

grounding: An older sibling watches a five-year-old brother try a first lie for a treat, testing whether an adult can see into his mind.

passage:
Monday. Sarita found red scribbles all over Sachin's new colouring book. "Baby did it," Sachin said quickly. His sister was one and had been asleep in her cot all afternoon. Sarita raised an eyebrow and only said, "Hmm."
Wednesday. The biscuit packet was open. "Not me," said Sachin, watching his mother's face closely. Sarita said, "I think you wanted a biscuit. You can ask me."
Friday. Juice spilled on the sofa. Sachin opened his mouth, stopped, and grinned sheepishly. "Me. I spilled it." Sarita hugged him. "Thank you for telling me. Let's get a cloth."

qa.q: Who did Sachin blame for the scribbles?
qa.a: He said, "Baby did it," though his sister was one and asleep in her cot.

qa.q: How was Sachin feeling as he watched his mother's face so closely on Wednesday?
qa.a: Sachin was probably nervous about being found out, watching her face to test whether she could tell what he had done.

qa.q: What did Sarita do that made the truth easier by Friday?
qa.a: She stayed calm, named what he wanted, told him he could ask, and thanked him when he admitted the spill.

qa.q: What would change if Sarita had shouted on Monday?
qa.a: Sachin might have learned to hide mistakes better instead of trying the truth by Friday.

grounding: Over a week a preschool boy tries simple lies to avoid trouble or get a treat, a sign of growing understanding of other minds, and his mother responds calmly.

passage:
Mumma had gone to the market, and big sister Ankita was in charge.
Akash walked into the kitchen and stood very straight. "Mumma said I can have ice cream. Two scoops."
Ankita raised an eyebrow. "When did she say that?"
"Before. When you were in the bathroom." He blinked slowly, watching her face to see if it was working.
Ankita smiled. She remembered doing the same thing at his age. She picked up her phone. "Let's ask Mumma together."
Akash's face fell. "Maybe she said one scoop."
Mumma's voice on the phone laughed. "Nice try, Akash. After dinner. One scoop."
Akash sighed and went back to his blocks, already thinking.

qa.q: How many scoops did Mumma agree to after dinner?
qa.a: One scoop.

qa.q: Why did Akash watch Ankita's face?
qa.a: Akash felt hopeful and a bit nervous, checking whether she believed his story, because he had realised she couldn't see what Mumma really said.

qa.q: How did Ankita handle the lie?
qa.a: Ankita stayed calm and checked by calling Mumma together, without shaming him.

qa.q: How does Ankita see Akash's lie?
qa.a: Ankita finds it a little funny and familiar, remembering doing the same at his age.

grounding: It shows a preschooler trying his first strategic lie for a treat, aware the adult cannot see his mind, and an older sister handling it calmly.

passage:
"Imran, did you brush your teeth?" Manoj Uncle called from the next room. He was looking after Imran while Ammi was at work.
"Yes!" Imran said. He hadn't. He was lying on the bed with his toy truck.
"Really?"
"Really really."
Manoj Uncle came in, holding the toothbrush. "Hmm. Your brush is dry."
Imran looked at the brush. Then at Uncle. "I brushed with… no water."
Manoj Uncle laughed softly. "You thought I couldn't tell, na? Clever boy. But teeth need real brushing. Come, I'll do mine too."
Imran slid off the bed. "Can I do the bubbles first?"
"You can do the bubbles first."

qa.q: What did Manoj Uncle notice about the toothbrush?
qa.a: Your brush is dry.

qa.q: Why did Imran say he brushed with no water?
qa.a: Imran felt caught and a little worried, and quickly tried a new story because he was learning Uncle couldn't see inside his head.

qa.q: How did Manoj Uncle respond wisely?
qa.a: He stayed calm and warm, named what he could see, and made brushing fun by doing it together.

qa.q: How does Manoj Uncle see Imran's lie?
qa.a: He sees it as a clever step in growing up rather than a moral failure, which is why he laughs softly.

grounding: It shows a preschooler trying a lie to avoid brushing, a sign of growing understanding of other minds, and a calm adult response.

passage:
Preschool note, Friday, Blue Room.
Today Suraj told me that Manjula had taken his sticker, hoping for a new one. Manjula said she hadn't. I had seen Suraj put the sticker in his own pocket a minute earlier.
I didn't call him a liar. At this age, trying out a lie is a sign that children are learning others can't see inside their heads. It's a step, not a failing.
I crouched and said, "I think your sticker might be in your pocket. Can you check?" He checked, went pink and giggled. Then he said sorry to Manjula without being asked.
I'll let his family know how gently he took it back.

qa.q: Where had Suraj put the sticker?
qa.a: In his own pocket.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he checked his pocket?
qa.a: Suraj felt caught and a little embarrassed, going pink and giggling.

qa.q: How did the teacher respond to Suraj's lie?
qa.a: The teacher avoided calling him a liar and gave him a gentle chance to check his pocket and make it right himself.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt when Suraj blamed her?
qa.a: Manjula probably felt confused and upset at being blamed, and relieved when he said sorry.

grounding: A preschool teacher notes a child's first strategic lie for a sticker and treats it as a developmental step, not moral failure.

passage:
At the sweet shop behind the bus stand in Rewari, Kamal dada was sharing out laddoos. "Only for clean hands," he said.
Five-year-old Dhruv had been playing with the stray puppy. His hands were grey. He hid them behind his back and said, "I washed them. With soap."
Dada looked at him. Dhruv looked back, very serious, testing. Could dada tell?
"Show me," dada said gently.
Dhruv brought his hands out slowly. He grinned, caught. "Puppy hands."
Dada laughed and led him to the tap. "Real washing gets a real laddoo."

qa.q: What had Dhruv been playing with?
qa.a: The stray puppy.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he looked back at dada so seriously?
qa.a: Dhruv was curious and hopeful, testing whether dada could tell what he had really done.

qa.q: How did Kamal dada handle the fib?
qa.a: He stayed gentle, asked to see the hands, laughed when Dhruv was caught, and led him to the tap so real washing earned the laddoo.

qa.q: What might dada understand about Dhruv's fib?
qa.a: Dada seems to see it as a small child's first try at a trick, a normal step in growing up, not something to punish.

grounding: Shows a preschooler trying a first strategic fib to get a treat, testing whether the adult can see his mind, as a normal developmental step.
